Protecting the Undeleted in Machine Unlearning

Aloni Cohen ††thanks: University of Chicago. <aloni@uchicago.edu>.    Refael Kohen ††thanks: Tel Aviv University. <refael.kohen@gmail.com>. Partially supported by the Israel Science Foundation (grant 1419/24) and the Blavatnik Family Foundation.    Kobbi Nissim ††thanks: Dept. of Computer Science, Georgetown University. <kobbi.nissim@georgetown.edu>. Work partly supported by NSF award #2217678.    Uri Stemmer ††thanks: Tel Aviv University. <u@uri.co.il>. Partially supported by the Israel Science Foundation (grant 1419/24) and the Blavatnik Family Foundation.
February 18, 2026
Abstract

Machine unlearning aims to remove specific data points from a trained model, often striving to emulate “perfect retraining”, i.e., producing the model that would have been obtained had the deleted data never been included. We demonstrate that this approach, and security definitions that enable it, carry significant privacy risks for the remaining (undeleted) data points. We present a reconstruction attack showing that for certain tasks, which can be computed securely without deletions, a mechanism adhering to perfect retraining allows an adversary controlling merely ω⁡(1)\omega(1) data points to reconstruct almost the entire dataset merely by issuing deletion requests. We survey existing definitions for machine unlearning, showing they are either susceptible to such attacks or too restrictive to support basic functionalities like exact summation. To address this problem, we propose a new security definition that specifically safeguards undeleted data against leakage caused by the deletion of other points. We show that our definition permits several essential functionalities, such as bulletin boards, summations, and statistical learning.

1 Introduction

Sensitive personal data underlies the training of machine learning models across many domains, necessitating compliance with legal data protection standards such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA). These legal standards provide individuals with a number of protections and rights, including the right to request that their specific information be deleted, a.k.a. the Right to be Forgotten (RTBF). This legal provision gave rise to the field of Machine Unlearning, a branch of machine learning focused on enabling the removal of elements from the training data without needing to rebuild models from scratch.

We now make our discussion more formal and survey several influential definitions for machine unlearning. Consider a data curator 𝒞\mathcal{C} that executes an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} on an initial input dataset D0=(x1,…,xn)D_{0}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) to obtain an outcome h0h_{0} (say a hypothesis or a statistic). Throughout the execution, at every time ii, the curator 𝒞\mathcal{C} receives a deletion request of the form “delete point xjx_{j}” and needs to respond with an updated outcome hih_{i} that should reflect the state of the dataset after this iith deletion request. Starting from the work of Cao and Yang (2015), machine unlearning was defined as a computational problem, where the ideal solution is for the curator to retrain the learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} from scratch in every step on the remaining dataset. The goal of the machine unlearning algorithm is to emulate this ideal solution (perfectly or approximately) faster, i.e., without having to spend the work needed to re-run 𝒜\mathcal{A} for every deletion request. For example, if 𝒜\mathcal{A} returns the exact sum h0=x1+⋯+xnh_{0}=x_{1}+\cdots+x_{n}, deleting xjx_{j} could be done via a single subtraction h1=h0−xjh_{1}=h_{0}-x_{j} (instead of summing the nn numbers again). This way, deletion is performed in constant rather than linear time.

Following Cao and Yang (2015), several other definitions were suggested, including by Ginart et al. (2019); Guo et al. (2019); Sekhari et al. (2021); Gupta et al. (2021), with the same goal of mimicking/approximating the behavior of retraining from scratch in every iteration (“the ideal solution”) while saving on runtime. These definitions differ in the approximation metrics they consider and in their environmental settings (such as whether or not the deletion requests are adaptive to past outputs). The focus of our work is not on runtime; therefore, for our purposes, all these definitions can be grouped together as definitions that are satisfied by perfect retraining. See Section 1.2 for a survey of prior definitions.

Perfect retraining and privacy.

While the right to delete one’s information is rooted in privacy standards such as the GDPR, the relationship between data deletion and privacy is not straightforward. In particular, it is well-known that definitions satisfied by perfect retraining fail under a simple “differencing attack” where an adversary learns information about the deleted item by examining the output hypothesis before and after a deletion (e.g., in the exact sum example, if an attacker sees the outcome before and after Alice deletes her input, then the attacker learns Alice’s input exactly).

Nevertheless, one may argue that such compromise of Alice’s personal data is acceptable as long as Alice is aware of her privacy risks and still wants to exercise control over her data and delete it from the model. However, as we will see, there are cases where the deletion of Alice’s data can compromise the privacy of other users who did not ask for their data to be deleted. More generally, we will show that there are tasks for which any machine unlearning mechanism, under any definition satisfied by perfect retraining, allows an attacker controlling a small number of parties to reconstruct essentially all the training data. This, we believe, should be prevented.

Privacy-oriented definitions of deletion.

There are several privacy-oriented definitions in the literature that are not satisfied by perfect retraining (and thus might not be susceptible to our attacks). Perhaps the first example of such a (folklore) definition would be one that requires the use of differential privacy (DP) with small enough privacy parameters to capture group privacy for all the deleted users.11 1 That is, at the outset of the execution, the curator releases some DP computation on the initial dataset (with very small privacy parameters) and then simply ignores all deletion requests. However, to the best of our knowledge, all existing definitions that are not satisfied by perfect retraining are too restrictive in the sense that they disallow natural and important functionalities, such as a simple sum or a bulletin board. Again, we refer the reader to Section 1.2 for a survey of prior definitions.

1.1 Our contributions

Perfect retraining allows exposure of undeleted elements.

We present settings in which a coalition of a small number of parties can reconstruct the information of other parties by issuing data deletion requests. In the simplest setting, one party, Alice, who asks for her data to be deleted, causes the information of another party, who did not ask for their data to be deleted, to be exposed. In this scenario: (i) Alice could not learn the other party’s data had she not deleted her data, and (ii) Alice can learn the other party’s data once the deletion is performed. We believe that enabling such behavior is unacceptable; thus, we argue that definitions that aim to mimic or approximate perfect retraining should be used with caution.

A simple example where the deletion of one party’s data causes another’s to be revealed is in median computation. Given nn data points x1≤x2≤⋯≤xnx_{1}\leq x_{2}\leq\cdots\leq x_{n} their median is xn+12x_{\frac{n+1}{2}} if nn is odd and xn2x_{\frac{n}{2}} otherwise. Observe that the initial median computation reveals one data point. Assume nn is odd and that Alice’s entry is greater than the median. When Alice asks to delete her data, a value smaller than the median is exposed – the input provided by some another user. (See Appendix A for another example).

The median example is perhaps somewhat controversial because the exact median itself is a highly non-private computation even without any deletions. Thus, one might argue that the privacy violation generated in this context is more because of the functionality itself rather than because of the deletions.22 2 Taking this argument to the limit, consider the functionality ff where given a dataset DD we have that f⁡(D)=∅f(D)=\emptyset if |D|≥n|D|\geq n, and f⁡(D)=Df(D)=D otherwise. Now, if the initial dataset is of size nn, then by deleting her data Alice causes the function ff to leak all of the (remaining) dataset. However, in Section 2 we present a task which can be performed with differential privacy (without supporting deletions). Nevertheless, an attacker controlling only a small number of parties, asking them to delete their data one by one, would force any perfect-retraining algorithm to leak almost all of its dataset.

Theorem 1.1 (informal).

There exists a task TT such that

  1. (1)

    There exists an (o⁡(1),o⁡(1))\left(o(1),o(1)\right)-differentially private algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that for any dataset DD we have that 𝒜⁡(D)\mathcal{A}(D) solves TT w.r.t. DD with high probability.

  2. (2)

    Perfect retraining w.r.t. TT allows an attacker controlling merely ω⁡(1)\omega(1) points to reconstruct almost all of the dataset. Specifically, there is an attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} and a set of points B={b1,…,br}B=\{b_{1},\dots,b_{r}\} of size |B|=ω⁡(1)|B|=\omega(1) such that the following holds. (BB is the set of points controlled by ℬ\mathcal{B}.) For any dataset DD containing BB, and any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for TT, given (𝒜⁡(D),𝒜⁡(D∖{b1}),𝒜⁡(D∖{b1,b2}),…,𝒜⁡(D∖B))\left(\mathcal{A}(D),\mathcal{A}(D\setminus\{b_{1}\}),\mathcal{A}(D\setminus\{b_{1},b_{2}\}),\dots,\mathcal{A}(D\setminus B)\right), the attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} can reconstruct almost all of DD.

By item (1), without deletions, the task TT can be solved while guaranteeing strong privacy protections for the input dataset. Nevertheless, by item (2), an attacker that controls merely ω⁡(1)\omega(1) points and can request their deletion from the dataset can reconstruct almost all of the dataset (reconstruct ≈n\approx n points by deleting ω⁡(1)\omega(1) points). As we mentioned, many existing definitions for machine unlearning are satisfied by perfect retraining. Theorem 1.1 shows that these definitions do not rule out mechanisms that leak their entire dataset after just ω⁡(1)\omega(1) deletion requests.

Remark 1.2.

Item (1) of Theorem 1.1 is stated with (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP for δ=o⁡(1)\delta=o(1). This is not standard, but still prevents the attacker from reconstructing, say, 1% of the rows in DD. The formal details are given in Appendix B. In particular, this can be restated with arbitrary (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta) parameters, at the cost requiring the attacker described in Item (2) to control ω⁡(log⁡(1/δ)ε2)\omega\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right) points.

A new definition for deletion safety.

Motivated by these vulnerabilities, we propose a new framework for machine unlearning. Unlike prior definitions that focus on removing the influence of the deleted point to mimic a world where it never existed, our definition focuses on protecting the privacy of the remaining, undeleted elements. Informally, we require that an attacker who observes an initial model and submits a sequence of deletion requests gains no additional information about the remaining dataset beyond what is inherent in the initial model and the deleted values themselves. We formalize this via a simulation-based definition, and provide variants handling non-adaptive and adaptive adversaries, as well as a relaxation allowing for bounded leakage.

Examples satisfying our new definition.

We show that our new definition is satisfied by stateless algorithms. This allows us to show that the exact sum and the bulletin board functionalities, which were disallowed by previous rigorous definitions, are compatible with our definition. Furthermore, we provide examples for mechanisms, which were studied by prior work under the umbrella of perfect retraining, that are nevertheless compatible with our new definition. In other words, even though our work highlights security vulnerabilities of perfect retraining as a security notion, this does not necessarily mean that existing algorithms in the literature are bad; indeed, some of them could be justified using our new security notion.

1.2 A survey of prior definitions

Definitions that are satisfied by perfect retraining.

Our attacks apply to all definitions which are satisfied by perfect retraining. This includes all the definitions in the literature in which perfect retraining is the “stated goal”/“optimum” Cao and Yang (2015); Ginart et al. (2019); Guo et al. (2019); Sekhari et al. (2021); Gupta et al. (2021). It also includes definitions where retraining from scratch is sufficient even if not the stated goal.

One such definition, called deletion-as-control, was introduced by Cohen et al. (2023a). Recall that we consider a data curator 𝒞\mathcal{C} that holds an initial dataset DD and sequentially receives deletion requests for elements from DD (and updates its responses accordingly). Informally, deletion-as-control requires that the internal state of the curator 𝒞\mathcal{C} in the real-world (where, say, Alice contributes her information and then asks to delete it) would be distributed similarly to its state in a “hypothetical world” where Alice does not contribute her data in the first place, but all other parties (except the curator) behave as if she did. Note that this definition is satisfied by perfect retraining because in perfect retraining the curator need not have a state besides the dataset, which is identical in the two executions (after the deletion).

Another notable definition by Godin and Lamontagne (2021) requires that the internal state of the curator 𝒞\mathcal{C} after Alice deletes her data should be simulatable from the view of all other parties (except Alice and the curator). Note that perfect retraining satisfies this definition, because the curator does not have a state besides the dataset, which consists of information jointly held by the parties excluding Alice.

Definitions that are too restrictive.

Not all definitions are satisfied by perfect retraining; against these our attacks do not apply. As we argue next, these definitions can be too restrictive in some settings. In particular, all the definitions we discuss next rule out simple and important functionalities including exact sums and bulletin board Cohen et al. (2023a). As a concrete example to have in mind, a bulletin board should allow users to publicly post messages and to later remove them.

Perhaps the most influential definition in this context, called deletion-as-compliance, was introduced by Garg et al. (2020). Suppose that Alice contributes and later deletes her data by interacting with the curator 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Informally, the requirement in the definition of Garg et al. (2020) is that both the internal state of the curator 𝒞\mathcal{C} as well as the view of all other parties (except the curator and Alice) should be distributed similarly to the way they would have been distributed in an ideal world in which Alice never contributed her data in the first place. This means, in particular, that the view of these other parties (capturing everything they see throughout the execution) cannot be affected by Alice. Bulletin boards and exact sums are impossible: the view of other parties is inherently affected by Alice’s contribution.

This issue was addressed by Gao et al. (2022) who presented a weaker variant of the definition of Garg et al. (2020) with the goal of being more permissive. Informally, the definition of Gao et al. (2022) is as follows. Suppose that Alice contributes two records and later deletes one of them (by interacting with the curator 𝒞\mathcal{C}). The requirement is that all other parties together should not be able to distinguish (based on their view of the execution) whether Alice deleted the first or the second record. This definition is indeed more permissive and, in particular, permits the fact that a deletion has occurred to be visible (but the identify of the deleted record needs to be kept hidden). However, this definition still rules out the exact sum and the bulletin board functionalities for the same reasons as above.

Finally, Chourasia and Shah (2023) studied privacy risks that may arise when the adversary that selects the sequence of deletion requests is adaptive to the prior outputs of the curator.33 3 This work extends the work of Gupta et al. (2021) that we mentioned above. Gupta et al. (2021) also studied adaptivity in machine unlearning, tackling the concern that algorithms that aim to mimic perfect retraining efficiently might lose their guarantees when the sequence of deletion is selected adaptively. Their work was motivated by observation that if the sequence of deletions is adaptive, then this sequence itself might continue to reveal information about a record even after this record was deleted from the system. Informally, their definition requires that for every adaptive adversary QQ (that adaptively specifies deletion requests), every initial dataset DD, every record y∈Dy\in D, and every time step ii, the output of the curator after receiving i−1i-1 deletion requests from QQ and then a request to delete yy is simulatable from D∖{y}D\setminus\{y\}.44 4 More specifically, their definition requires that for every adaptive adversary QQ and every time step ii there exists a simulator πiQ\pi^{Q}_{i} such that the following holds. For every initial dataset DD and every record y∈Dy\in D, the output distribution of the curator at time ii, after receiving i−1i-1 deletion requests (chosen adaptively by QQ) and then receiving a request to delete yy, is similar to the outcome distribution of the simulator πiQ​(D∖{y})\pi^{Q}_{i}\left(D\setminus\{y\}\right). Notice that the simulator of Chourasia and Shah (2023) is given all the data except for a single record, including every undeleted record. This if very much at odds with the ethos of our goal of privacy for those who remain.

Still, as Chourasia and Shah (2023) prove, the fact that this must hold for any adaptive adversary QQ forces the curator to provide some form of privacy protections to the records in DD. (Roughly, the functionality can be non-private for at most a single time step.) Thus it disallows simple functionalities such as the exact sum or the bulletin board. To see this for the bulletin board functionality, consider an adaptive QQ that behaves as follows: If Alice’s public message mentions Bob, then QQ will request to delete Alice then Bob. Otherwise, QQ will request to delete Alice then Charlie. Since the simulator is executed without Alice’s record, it cannot simulate which record to delete next.

Note that the definition of Chourasia and Shah (2023) argues about every single time step separately. In Section 2.2, we show that such definitions are vulnerable to a type of attack we call a generalized differencing attack.

2 Attacks

In this section, we present several attacks in which an attacker controlling some of the records in a dataset can use the ability to delete these records in order to learn information about other records in the dataset.

2.1 Reconstruction attacks

Let us reconsider the median example, with the goal of releasing an approximate median rather than the exact median. Specifically, consider an algorithm that given a dataset DD returns a differentially private (DP) approximation for the median. This breaks the attack described in Section 1.1, as it prevents the attacker from directly learning information about the remaining points from their DP median. Still, by deleting more and more points the attacker gets to see more and more releases (approximate medians), which together might allow it to infer information about the remaining points. If we were to ensure that all releases together satisfy DP, as in the continual observation model of Dwork et al. (2010), then this would provably prevent such an attack. However, this can come at a high price in terms of utility. Specifically, Jain et al. (2023) presented problems that can be solved efficiently with differential privacy in the single shot setting (where only one output is released), but not in the continual setting, where the input dataset evolves over time and DP must be preserved across all outputs together.

We now briefly describe a variant of one of the attacks of Jain et al. (2023), tailored to our setting. Essentially, the only conceptual modification from the attacks presented by Jain et al. (2023) is that we highlight the fact that it is not just that DP cannot be maintained in this continual setting, but it is in fact the privacy of ‘‘undeleted’’ points that get compromised.55 5 This also holds in the attacks of Jain et al. (2023), but not explicit as this was not their focus; they aimed to show that the error must be large as a function of the size of the evolving dataset (which includes both the deleted and undeleted elements in our context). This will not yet result in the attack described in Theorem 1.1 as the number of users that the attacker needs to control will be relatively large. Consider the following problem: Given a multiset T⊆[n]T\subseteq[n], the goal is to return an approximation to

CountMod(T)≜∑i∈[n]𝟙{countT(i)mod 3=2},{\rm CountMod}(T)\triangleq\sum_{i\in[n]}\mathds{1}\Big\{{\rm count}_{T}(i)\;{\rm mod}\;3=2\Big\},

where countT​(i){\rm count}_{T}(i) is the number of occurrences of ii in TT. Note that CountMod{\rm CountMod} is a function of sensitivity 1, and hence could be approximated with DP (in the single shot setting) with error roughly 1/ε1/\varepsilon.

Now consider a dataset (multiset) T=D∪S⊆[n]T=D\cup S\subseteq[n], where DD is a random subset of [n][n] of size n/2n/2, and where SS is the multiset of size 3​n23n^{2} containing 3​n3n copies of every i∈[n]i\in[n]. We consider an attacker that “controls” SS (in the sense that it can request the deletion of points from SS) and aims to learn the dataset DD. Now observe that by controlling SS, the attacker can force any mechanism for CountMod{\rm CountMod} to provide it with answers to counting queries w.r.t. DD. In more detail, a counting query is defined via a predicate q:[n]→{0,1}q:[n]\rightarrow\{0,1\}, and the value of such a query on DD is q⁡(D)≜∑i∈Dq⁡(i)q(D)\triangleq\sum_{i\in D}q(i). Given such a counting query qq, the attacker acts as follows:

  1. 1.

    For every i∈[n]i\in[n] such that q⁡(i)=1q(i)=1, request the deletion of 2 copies of ii from SS (and thus from TT).

  2. 2.

    Obtain a release aq≈CountMod⁡(T)a_{q}\approx{\rm CountMod}(T). Note that CountMod⁡(T)=q⁡(D){\rm CountMod}(T)=q(D), because, by Step 1, for every i∈[n]i\in[n] such that q⁡(i)=0q(i)=0 we have that countT​(i)​mod​ 3≠2{\rm count}_{T}(i)\;{\rm mod}\;3\neq 2, and for every i∈[n]i\in[n] such that q⁡(i)=1q(i)=1 we have that countT​(i)​mod​ 3=2{\rm count}_{T}(i)\;{\rm mod}\;3=2 if and only if i∈Di\in D.

Further reducing the number of deletions.

We can further reduce the number of points that the attacker controls (and deletes) by modifying the task such that the algorithm is required to release approximate answers to multiple queries together, rather than just one. The upside here is that the attacker needs to control very few points (ω⁡(1)\omega(1) points) and by deleting them the attacker can reconstruct a dataset of size nn. This results in Theorem 1.1. The formal details are given in Appendix B.

2.2 Generalized differencing attacks

As we mentioned, definitions that aim to mimic/approximate the behavior of perfect retraining are susceptible to “differencing attacks”, such as the simple counting example, where seeing two consecutive releases (before and after a deletion) allows the attacker to learn the deleted point. We now present simple generalizations of this attack that extend to other types of definitions:

  1. 1.

    Consider a learning algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes a dataset DD containing nn numbers, represented in binary (say using dd bits). The algorithm ignores the data and returns a random binary vector of length dd, denoted as zz. Next, upon receiving a request to delete a point xx, the algorithm deletes xx from the data and returns z⊕xz\oplus x. This, of course, allows the same “differencing attack”. However, note that now the marginal distribution of every single release given by the algorithm is simply uniform over dd-bit vectors, independent of the data. This shows that definitions that only argue about every single time step individually, like the definition of Chourasia and Shah (2023) mentioned above, can be vulnerable to differencing attacks even if they require that the distribution of every release is independent of the data.66 6 For this we need to assume that either the curator is allowed to hold a state (the vector zz), or that the deletion algorithm receives an input both the point to be deleted (the point xx) and the previous release (the vector zz in our case).

  2. 2.

    Somewhat artificially, a similar attack could be leveraged to reveal information about “undeleted” points. The attack begins the same, with the initial release being a random dd-bit vector zz. Next, upon receiving a request to delete a point xx, the algorithm deletes xx from the data, samples a random point yy from the remaining data points, and returns z⊕yz\oplus y.

3 Our new definition(s)

Consider a setting where a curator wishes to compute a functionality ff on an initial dataset DD while supporting ongoing deletion requests. We present security definitions that specifically safeguard undeleted data against leakage caused by the deletion of other points. We conceptually separate our focus from the following two types of privacy risks:

  1. 1.

    Our security definition does not address privacy risks that are inherent to the functionality ff itself. This mirrors the paradigm of secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) in cryptography: an MPC protocol guarantees that nothing is leaked beyond the output of the chosen function ff, but whether evaluating ff is acceptable from a privacy standpoint is left as an external, system-level choice. We adopt a similar philosophy, accepting that the initial release of f⁡(D)f(D), before any deletion is made, may inherently reveal information about DD. We instead wish to limit the information subsequently revealed by deleting elements, not taking for granted the leakage that would come from recomputing ff after each request.

  2. 2.

    We separate the risks incurred to deleted points from the risks incurred to undeleted points. As we mentioned, the machine unlearning community is already well-aware that there are cases where, by deleting her data, Alice exposes herself to privacy risks (such as in a differencing attack). Nevertheless, Alice should have the right to make a calculated, informed decision to delete her data even in the face of such risks.

Our point is not that leakage via ff itself or w.r.t. deleted points is unimportant. Rather, we argue that even if we accept these two types of leakage, there are still other critical risks that need to be addressed. Specifically, our work focuses on the scenario where some users’ deletions compromise the privacy of the remaining users who never opted to delete their data. Our goal is to formulate a security definition guaranteeing that Bob’s privacy is not harmed by other people deleting their data, beyond what is inherently revealed about Bob’s data from the initial release and the value of the deleted points (which the adversary may learn).

3.1 Non-adaptive attacker

We start with the simplest variant of our definition that handles non-adaptive attackers who decide on the sequence of deletions ahead of time. To simplify the presentation, we do not distinguish between the “algorithm” and the “curator” and consider one stateful algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following syntax. Initially 𝒜\mathcal{A} is executed on a dataset DD and outputs an initial output z0←𝒜⁡(D)z_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(D). Then, for kk rounds i=1,2,…,ki=1,2,\dots,k, algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} obtains a point yi∈Dy_{i}\in D and returns a modified output zi←𝒜⁡(D,y1,…,yi)z_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1},\dots,y_{i}). The mindset is that ziz_{i} represents the result of “deleting” yiy_{i} from DD, but this is not part of the formal definition. We also write (𝒜⁡(D),𝒜⁡(D,y1),𝒜⁡(D,y1,y2),…,𝒜⁡(D,y1,y2,…,yk))\left(\mathcal{A}(D),\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1}),\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1},y_{2}),\dots,\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{k})\right) to denote the vector of outcomes obtained by running 𝒜\mathcal{A} on DD and then “deleting” one by one the points y1,…,yky_{1},\dots,y_{k}.77 7 We stress that algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} can have an internal state, which is omitted from this vector notation for simplicity.

Definition 3.1 (Non-adaptive variant).

Algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is kk-undeleted-safe if there is a simulator Sim{\rm Sim} such that for every dataset DD of size nn, and every sequence (y1,…,yk′)(y_{1},\dots,y_{k^{\prime}}) containing k′≤kk^{\prime}\leq k distinct points from DD it holds that

Sim⁡(𝒜⁡(D),y1,…,yk′)≈(𝒜⁡(D),𝒜⁡(D,y1),𝒜⁡(D,y1,y2),…,𝒜⁡(D,y1,y2,…,yk′)).{\rm Sim}(\mathcal{A}(D),y_{1},\dots,y_{k^{\prime}})\approx\left(\mathcal{A}(D),\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1}),\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1},y_{2}),\dots,\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{k^{\prime}})\right).

In words, there is a simulator that takes only the initial output 𝒜⁡(D)\mathcal{A}(D) and the values of the deleted points (y1,…,yk′)(y_{1},\dots,y_{k^{\prime}}), and can simulate the entire sequence of updated outputs generated by 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Intuitively, this formalizes the goal stated above: an attacker observing the entire sequence of unlearning updates learns nothing more about the remaining dataset than what they could already compute themselves from the initial release and the deleted values.

Remark 3.2.

Definition 3.1 can be instantiated with any notion of similarity between the distributions, such as statistical indistinguishability, computational indistinguishability, or the similarity notion used by differential privacy.

3.2 Static adaptive attacker

We now extend the definition to the case where an attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} can adaptively decide on the order of deletions. The attacker is static in the sense that the points it controls (and is allowed to delete) are predetermined. We assume that there are no other deletions in the game. In addition, the attacker might possess some side-information about the other points in the dataset DD, which we denote as SideInfo⁡(D){\rm SideInfo}(D). Formally, for a dataset D=(x1,…,xn)D=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}), a set Y⊆[n]Y\subseteq[n] of size k′≤kk^{\prime}\leq k denoting the indices of the points in DD controlled by ℬ\mathcal{B}, and a side-information function SideInfo{\rm SideInfo}, we consider the following game between algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the attacker ℬ\mathcal{B}:

  1. 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐆𝐚𝐦𝐞⁡(𝓐,𝑫=(𝒙𝟏,…,𝒙𝒏),𝓑,𝒀⊆[𝒏],𝐒𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨):¯\underline{\boldsymbol{{\rm StaticGame}(\mathcal{A},\,D{=}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),\,\mathcal{B},\,Y{\subseteq}[n],\,{\rm SideInfo}){:}}}

  2. 1.

    Let z0←𝒜⁡(D)z_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(D).

  3. 2.

    The attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} obtains the controlled points D|Y≜{(i,xi):i∈Y}D\big|_{Y}\triangleq\{(i,x_{i}):i\in Y\}, the side-information SideInfo⁡(D){\rm SideInfo}(D), and the initial output z0z_{0}.

  4. 3.

    For ℓ=1,2,…,|Y|\ell=1,2,\dots,|Y|:

    1. (a)

      The attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} chooses an index jℓ∈Y∖{j1,j2,…,jℓ−1}j_{\ell}\in Y\setminus\{j_{1},j_{2},\dots,j_{\ell-1}\}

    2. (b)

      Algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} receives a deletion request for the point xjℓx_{j_{\ell}} and returns an updated output zℓz_{\ell}, which is given to ℬ\mathcal{B}.

  5. 4.

    The attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} outputs its view of the interaction, which includes its internal randomness, the indices of the controlled points YY, its side-information SideInfo⁡(D){\rm SideInfo}(D), and all the outputs it received from 𝒜\mathcal{A} during the interaction.

Definition 3.3 (Static adaptive variant).

Algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is kk-undeleted-safe if for every attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} there is a simulator Sim{\rm Sim} such that for every side-information function SideInfo{\rm SideInfo}, every dataset DD of size nn, and every set of indices Y⊆[n]Y\subseteq[n] of size |Y|≤k|Y|\leq k it holds that

Sim⁡(𝒜⁡(D),D|Y,SideInfo)≈StaticGame⁡(𝒜,D,ℬ,Y,SideInfo).{\rm Sim}\left(\mathcal{A}(D),D\big|_{Y},{\rm SideInfo}\right)\approx{\rm StaticGame}\left(\mathcal{A},D,\mathcal{B},Y,{\rm SideInfo}\right).

Note that any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies Definition 3.3 also satisfies Definition 3.1, i.e., Definition 3.3 is (perhaps) harder to obtain. This holds by taking ℬ\mathcal{B} to be the attacker that fixes the ordering of the deletions from YY before the interaction begins, and setting SideInfo{\rm SideInfo} to be empty.

3.3 Dynamic adaptive attacker

In the previous two definitions, the set of indices/points that the attacker controlled was fixed ahead of time. We now handle the case where the attacker can dynamically choose the indices to control and delete. So now YY, the set of indices controlled by the attacker, is not fixed in advance. It is initially empty, and throughout the execution, the attacker dynamically decides on indices from [n][n] to “corrupt”. Once corrupted, these indices are added to YY. Formally, given a dataset D=(x1,…,xn)D=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}) we consider the following game between a stateful algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} and an attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} with side-information function SideInfo{\rm SideInfo}. This game has two modes, parameterized by the bit b∈{0,1}b\in\{0,1\}, where b=0b=0 corresponds to a “real world” execution in which the attacker learns the sequence of modified outputs of 𝒜\mathcal{A} after every deletion, and where b=1b=1 corresponds to an “ideal world” execution in which this information is hidden from the attacker.

  1. 𝐃𝐲𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐜𝐆𝐚𝐦𝐞𝒃​(𝓐,𝓑^,𝑫=(𝒙𝟏,…,𝒙𝒏),𝐒𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨):¯\underline{\boldsymbol{{\rm DynamicGame}_{b}(\mathcal{A},\,\hat{\mathcal{B}},\,D{=}(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}),\,{\rm SideInfo}){:}}}

  2. 1.

    Let ℓ=0\ell=0 and z0←𝒜⁡(D)z_{0}\leftarrow\mathcal{A}(D).

  3. 2.

    The attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} obtains SideInfo⁡(D){\rm SideInfo}(D) and the initial output z0z_{0}.

  4. 3.

    Initiate Y=R=∅Y=R=\emptyset. % Here YY denotes the set of indices controlled by the attacker, and RR denotes the indices it had already deleted.

  5. 4.

    While |R|<k|R|<k and the attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} has not ended the loop:

    1. (a)

      Set ℓ←ℓ+1\ell\leftarrow\ell+1.

    2. (b)

      The attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} chooses a set of indices Iℓ⊆[n]I_{\ell}\subseteq[n], possibly empty, under the restriction that |Y∪Iℓ|≤k|Y\cup I_{\ell}|\leq k, and learns xix_{i} for every i∈Iℓi\in I_{\ell}. Set Y←Y∪IℓY\leftarrow Y\cup I_{\ell}.

    3. (c)

      The attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} chooses a set of indices Jℓ⊆Y∖RJ_{\ell}\subseteq Y\setminus R, possibly empty. Set R←R∪JℓR\leftarrow R\cup J_{\ell}.

    4. (d)

      If b=0b=0 and Jℓ≠∅J_{\ell}\neq\emptyset then 𝒜\mathcal{A} receives a deletion request for the points in JℓJ_{\ell} and returns an updated output zℓz_{\ell}, which is given to the attacker. If b=1b=1, do nothing.

    5. (e)

      The attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} chooses whether to continue or to end the loop.

  6. 5.

    The attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} outputs vv. % In a “real world” execution, where b=0b=0, this vv can be thought of as the view of the attacker ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} at the end of the execution. However, in an “ideal world” execution, where b=1b=1, we think of ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} as a simulator that aims to simulate some other attacker, and so the value vv is not necessarily the view of ℬ^\hat{\mathcal{B}} itself, but rather a “simulated view” that should correspond to the view of the simulated attacker at the end of a real world execution.

  7. 6.

    The output of the game is (Y,v)(Y,v). % We include YY in the output of the game to force the simulator (when b=1b=1) to choose its corruptions similarly to the real world attacker (when b=0b=0). Otherwise, for example, the simulator could corrupt kk indices and use them to simulate a real-world attacker that only corrupts k/2k/2 indices.

Definition 3.4 (Dynamic adaptive variant).

Algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is kk-undeleted-safe if for every attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} there is a simulator Sim{\rm Sim} such that for every side-information function SideInfo{\rm SideInfo} and every dataset DD of size nn it holds that

DynamicGame1​(𝒜,Sim,D,SideInfo)≈DynamicGame0​(𝒜,ℬ,D,SideInfo).{\rm DynamicGame}_{1}(\mathcal{A},{\rm Sim},D,{\rm SideInfo})\approx{\rm DynamicGame}_{0}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},D,{\rm SideInfo}).

Note that any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies Definition 3.4 also satisfies Definition 3.3, i.e., Definition 3.4 is (perhaps) harder to obtain. This holds by taking ℬ\mathcal{B} to be the attacker that fixes the set YY before the interaction begins.

4 Algorithms satisfying our definition and extensions

It is immediate from Definition 3.4 that it is satisfied by any stateless algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}, where by stateless we mean that for any DD and deleted points y1,…,yky_{1},\dots,y_{k} it holds that (𝒜⁡(D),𝒜⁡(D,y1),…,𝒜⁡(D,y1,y2,…,yk))\left(\mathcal{A}(D),\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1}),\dots,\mathcal{A}(D,y_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{k})\right) is strictly determined by (𝒜⁡(D),y1,…,yk)\left(\mathcal{A}(D),y_{1},\dots,y_{k}\right). This includes interesting functionalities like a bulletin board and exact summations. Note that 𝒜⁡(D)\mathcal{A}(D) does not have to be deterministic for this argument to go through.

Example 4.1.

Consider the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes a dataset containing nn numbers from [0,1][0,1] and returns a DP estimation for their summation. Then, upon receiving a deletion request for a point xix_{i}, the algorithm simply returns (z−xi)(z-x_{i}) where zz is the previously released sum. This algorithm is stateless, so it satisfies our new definition, and it provides DP w.r.t. undeleted points.

Note that this task can also be solved in the continual observation model using the classical “tree algorithm” of Dwork et al. (2010), which would guarantee DP for both the deleted and the undeleted points. However, this provably requires error that scales with Ω⁡(log⁡k)\Omega(\log k) (Cohen et al., 2024). The simple algorithm described in Example 4.1 shows that if we only want to provide privacy for undeleted points, then a single DP calculation (the initial noisy summation) suffices, resulting in error independent of kk.

It is also immediate from our definition that some algorithms/functionalities do not satisfy it. For example, as we mentioned, the exact median allows the attacker to learn undeleted points, and thus does not satisfy our new definition.88 8 To see this, consider a dataset DD containing 1010 copies of the point 0, one “middle” point ww which is either w=1/4w=1/4 or w=3/4w=3/4, and 1212 copies of the point 1. The exact median is 1. Suppose that the attacker controls one of the copies of 11 (so k=1k=1 in this example). By deleting this controlled point, the exact median becomes ww, which is then revealed to the attacker. But without deletions the simulator does not get any information about ww and hence could not conduct the simulation. So suppose that we are interested in computing such function ff that is not directly compatible with our framework. The question then becomes: “how much additional information is needed, beyond ff, in order for the simulation to become possible?”. For example, observe that if SideInfo{\rm SideInfo} contains all of DD (the side-information available to the simulator and the attacker), then simulating the exact median, or any other functionality, becomes trivial. We aim to quantify this “additional leakage” that suffices for simulation, and minimize it. In particular, in some cases, it might be reasonable to allow for additional leakage that satisfies DP. We can argue about the additional leakage via two primary approaches:

  1. (1)

    We could explicitly give the simulator some additional leakage function gg of the dataset DD, in order for the simulation to become possible. This has the benefit of making the leakage explicit; hopefully allowing us to argue about it more easily and try to minimize it.

  2. (2)

    Instead (or maybe in addition) to considering such a leakage function gg, it might also be useful to replace ff with a different function f^\hat{f} that approximates it in some sense while being more suited to our definitions.99 9 This is common practice in the literature on differential privacy: When designing private analogous to non-private computations, we typically compute noisy/approximate variants of the original functionality. Computing f^\hat{f} instead of ff might require less, or no, additional leakage (in the form of gg). However, this might introduce another type of leakage because in our definition we do not protect against leakage caused by the initial computation, which would now be according to f^\hat{f} instead of ff.

We formulate option (1) in the following definition.1010 10 For concreteness, we state this variant of the definition only w.r.t. Definition 3.4. The same can be said w.r.t. Definitions 3.3 and 3.1.

Definition 4.2 (Dynamic adaptive variant, with leakage).

Let gg be a leakage function. Algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is (k,g)(k,g)-undeleted-safe with leakage if for every attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} there is a simulator Sim⁡(⋅){\rm Sim}(\cdot) that takes an additional input and then plays in DynamicGame1{\rm DynamicGame}_{1} such that the following holds. For every side-information function SideInfo{\rm SideInfo} and every dataset DD of size nn it holds that

DynamicGame1​(𝒜,Sim⁡(g⁡(D)),D,SideInfo)≈DynamicGame0​(𝒜,ℬ,D,SideInfo).{\rm DynamicGame}_{1}(\mathcal{A},{\rm Sim}(g(D)),D,{\rm SideInfo})\approx{\rm DynamicGame}_{0}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B},D,{\rm SideInfo}).

Note that any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that is kk-undeleted-safe according to Definition 3.4 is also (k,g)(k,g)-undeleted-safe according to Definition 4.2 with g≡⊥g\equiv\bot. On the other extreme, for g⁡(D)=Dg(D)=D Definition 4.2 becomes trivial in the sense that any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} would be (k,g)(k,g)-undeleted-safe (this holds because if the simulator knows DD then it can simulate all of the execution of DynamicGame0{\rm DynamicGame}_{0}). When gg is “bounded”, say a DP function, then the definition might be considered reasonable.

4.1 Approximate median

Suppose that we are interested in an algorithm that initially takes a dataset DD containing nn elements from a domain XX and releases an approximation z0z_{0} to the median of DD. Then, for kk rounds, the algorithm receives the ii-th deletion request and outputs a modified answer ziz_{i}. We evaluate the approximation of the median for the (remaining) data at any given moment using its rank error. That is, if the current dataset is DiD_{i} and the algorithm returns an answer ziz_{i}, then the error of ziz_{i} w.r.t. DiD_{i} is defined as

errorDi⁡(zi):=|{x∈Di:x​ is strictly between ​zi​ and median​(Di)}|.\error_{D_{i}}(z_{i}):=\left|\{x\in D_{i}:x\text{ is strictly between }z_{i}\text{ and }\mbox{median}(D_{i})\}\right|.

We aim to design an algorithm for approximating the median, while satisfying our security definition, that guarantee small worst-case error across all their (k+1)(k+1) releases. Naively, one could solve this task by first computing and releasing the exact median, and then ignoring all deletion requests. This stateless algorithm satisfies our security definition and guarantees error at most kk deterministically. Alternatively, we could extend Example 4.1 to this setting as follows.

Example 4.3.

Consider the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that takes a dataset DD containing nn points from some ordered domain XX and operates as follows. Initially, 𝒜\mathcal{A} computes a differentially private data structure PP that provides approximate answers to range queries w.r.t. DD. Specifically, for every a≤b∈Xa\leq b\in X it ensures that P⁡(a,b)≈|{x∈D:a≤x≤b}|P(a,b)\approx|\{x\in D:a\leq x\leq b\}|.1111 11 There are several such constructions in the literature, e.g., by Beimel et al. (2013); Bun et al. (2015); Kaplan et al. (2020); Cohen et al. (2023b). Note that this, in particular, allows us to compute an approximate median of the dataset DD. Now, throughout the execution, we simply subtract deleted elements from the approximate counts given by PP. Specifically, at any moment throughout the execution, we estimate the number of (remaining) elements in a range [a,b][a,b] as P⁡(a,b)−#del​(a,b)P(a,b)-\#_{\rm del}(a,b), where #del​(a,b)\#_{\rm del}(a,b) denotes the (exact) number of deleted elements between aa and bb. As in Example 4.1, this provides DP w.r.t. undeleted points, without increasing the error introduced by PP.

4.2 A recipe for undeleted-safe algorithms

Example 4.3 suggests the following informal recipe for fitting a functionality ff to our framework:

  1. (1)

    Identify a set of sufficient statistics for the function ff.

  2. (2)

    Estimate these statistics with differential privacy.

  3. (3)

    Throughout the execution, maintain these statistics as a function of the deleted points.

Of course, this recipe is only useful when the set of sufficient statistics we identify is compatible with differential privacy. It turns out that this is indeed the case for some functionalities that were studied by prior work on machine unlearning.

In particular, Cao and Yang (2015) presented the following “SQ framework” for machine unlearning: Let ff be any function which can be computed in the non-adaptive statistical query (SQ) model. That is, there exists a collection of predicates CC such that for any dataset DD, the value of f⁡(D)f(D) can be computed by post-processing {∑x∈Dc⁡(x)}c∈C\{\sum_{x\in D}c(x)\}_{c\in C}, i.e., the sum of each of the predicates in CC on the elements in DD. As Cao and Yang (2015) showed, tracking {∑x∈Dc⁡(x)}c∈C\{\sum_{x\in D}c(x)\}_{c\in C} throughout the execution allows us to maintain the current value of ff without recomputing it from scratch. When |C||C| is relatively small, this results in an efficient algorithm for perfect retraining. This SQ framework is particularly suited for our definition, as computing the initial values of {∑x∈Dc⁡(x)}c∈C\{\sum_{x\in D}c(x)\}_{c\in C} can be done in a DP manner (again, assuming that |C||C| is small). Afterwards, as in Examples 4.1 and 4.3, we could update these values as a function of the deleted points alone.

Appendix A kk-means clustering on the line

Consider a perfect retraining algorithm for kk-means that, upon deletion, simply (re)runs Lloyd’s algorithm [Lloyd, 1982] on the remaining data points.1212 12 Recall that Lloyd’s algorithm for kk-means is an iterative refinement procedure that alternates between assigning data points to the nearest cluster center and updating the cluster centers to be the mean of their assigned points. These iterative refinement procedure continues until convergence (when assignments no longer change). Furthermore, for the sake of this example, let us consider the simple case where k=2k=2 and the data points are on the real line.

We consider the following experiment. Initially, a dataset DD containing nn points is sampled from some fixed (known) distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Then, α​n\alpha n random points from the dataset DD are given to an attacker 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We refer to these points as the points that the attacker controls, and denote them as A⊆DA\subseteq D. The game now continues in iteration where in every iteration:

  1. 1.

    The attacker 𝒜\mathcal{A} picks a point a∈A∩Da\in A\cap D and requests it to be deleted from DD.

  2. 2.

    We remove aa from DD, rerun Lloyd’s algorithm on DD to obtain a new tuple (c1′,c2′)(c^{\prime}_{1},c^{\prime}_{2}) and give this tuple to 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

The goal of the attacker is to identify points which it does not control, i.e., discover points from D∖AD\setminus A. We show empirically that this can be done successfully for several choices for the underlying distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, including the uniform distribution over an interval, and a mixture of two normal distributions.

The intuition behind the attack is as follows. Suppose that the attacker knows, in addition to the current cluster centers (c1,c2)(c_{1},c_{2}) also knew the sizes of the clusters (m1,m2)(m_{1},m_{2}), where m1+m2=|D|m_{1}+m_{2}=|D|. By deleting a point from AA which is larger than c2c_{2}, the attacker causes the right cluster to shift slightly to the left, thereby potentially causing points from the left cluster to ‘‘jump’’ to the right cluster. If it happens that exactly one point jumps between the clusters, then the attacker learns this point exactly, as it knows the previous and new averages (i.e., centers) of the left cluster (and we assumed that the attacker knows the cluster sizes). We show empirically that this indeed happens several times throughout the execution.1313 13 If more than one point jumps between the clusters, say rr points, then the attacker could heuristically delete a point from the other side of the line, thereby causing jj points to potentially jump in the other direction. The attack now works if j∈{1,r−1,r+1}j\in\{1,r-1,r+1\} since by looking at two consecutive jumps of r,r+1r,r+1 points the attacker could isolate a single point.

It remains, therefore, to explain how the attacker can learn the sizes of the clusters from the cluster centers. Suppose that by deleting a point a∗a^{*} from the right side of the line, the attacker caused both centers to change, from (c1old,c2old)(c_{1}^{\rm old},c_{2}^{\rm old}) to (c1new,c2new)(c_{1}^{\rm new},c_{2}^{\rm new}). Let m1old,m2old,m1new,m2newm_{1}^{\rm old},m_{2}^{\rm old},m_{1}^{\rm new},m_{2}^{\rm new} denote the sizes of the corresponding clusters before and after the change. Let PP denote the sum of the points that jumped from the left to the right cluster and let p=m1old−m1new=m2new−m2old+1p=m_{1}^{\rm old}-m_{1}^{\rm new}=m_{2}^{\rm new}-m_{2}^{\rm old}+1 denote the number jumping points, where the (+1)(+1) is because of the deleted point a∗a^{*}. Also let n=m1old+m2old=m1new+m2new+1n=m_{1}^{\rm old}+m_{2}^{\rm old}=m_{1}^{\rm new}+m_{2}^{\rm new}+1 denote the size of the dataset before the deletion, which is known to the attacker. We have that

P=m1old⋅c1old−m1new⋅c1new=m1old⋅c1old−(m1old−p)⋅c1new.P=m_{1}^{\rm old}\cdot c_{1}^{\rm old}-m_{1}^{\rm new}\cdot c_{1}^{\rm new}=m_{1}^{\rm old}\cdot c_{1}^{\rm old}-\left(m_{1}^{\rm old}-p\right)\cdot c_{1}^{\rm new}.

Now, the sum of the points in the right cluster, after the change, can be written in two ways: Either

m2new⋅c2new=(m2old−1+p)⋅c2new=(n−m1old−1+p)⋅c2new,m_{2}^{\rm new}\cdot c_{2}^{\rm new}=\left(m_{2}^{\rm old}-1+p\right)\cdot c_{2}^{\rm new}=\left(n-m_{1}^{\rm old}-1+p\right)\cdot c_{2}^{\rm new}, (2)

or it can be written as

m2old⋅c2old+P−a∗=(n−m1old)⋅c2old+m1old⋅c1old−(m1old−p)⋅c1new−a∗.m_{2}^{\rm old}\cdot c_{2}^{\rm old}+P-a^{*}=\left(n-m_{1}^{\rm old}\right)\cdot c_{2}^{\rm old}+m_{1}^{\rm old}\cdot c_{1}^{\rm old}-\left(m_{1}^{\rm old}-p\right)\cdot c_{1}^{\rm new}-a^{*}. (3)

Equating (2) and (3) we get one equation with two unknown variables, m1oldm_{1}^{\rm old} and pp. Isolating pp from this equation allows us to express pp as a function of m1oldm_{1}^{\rm old} as follows:

p\displaystyle p =m1old⋅(c1old−c1new−c2old+c2new)+n⋅(c2old−c2new)+c2new−a∗c2new−c1new\displaystyle=\frac{m_{1}^{\rm old}\cdot\left(c_{1}^{\rm old}-c_{1}^{\rm new}-c_{2}^{\rm old}+c_{2}^{\rm new}\right)+n\cdot(c_{2}^{\rm old}-c_{2}^{\rm new})+c_{2}^{\rm new}-a^{*}}{c_{2}^{\rm new}-c_{1}^{\rm new}}

Now recall that both pp and m1oldm_{1}^{\rm old} must be integers. Heuristically, by trying different values for m1oldm_{1}^{\rm old} until the resulting pp is an integer, we succeed in fining the correct values for pp and m1oldm_{1}^{\rm old}, and thus learn the sizes of the clusters exactly. The code for this simulation is available on GitHub.

Appendix B An attacker controlling 𝝎⁡(𝟏){\boldsymbol{\omega(1)}} points

In this section we give the formal details for an attack scenario in which the attacker controls (and deletes) merely ω⁡(1)\omega(1) points and is still able to reconstruct ≈n\approx n “uncontrolled” (or “undeleted”) points.

Definition B.1 (The batch queries (BQ) problem).

Let n,k,t∈ℕn,k,t\in\mathbb{N} and α,β∈[0,1]\alpha,\beta\in[0,1] be parameters, and let Q=(q1,…,qn)Q=(q_{1},\dots,q_{n}) be a collection of nn counting queries over [n][n]. That is, every qq is a predicate q:[n]→{0,1}q:[n]\rightarrow\{0,1\}. Let T⊆[n]∪{⋆}T\subseteq[n]\cup\{\star\} be a multiset and let a→∈ℝt\vec{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{t} be a real valued vector. We say that a→\vec{a} is α\alpha-accurate for TT if there exists an integer ii such that

⌈Star⁡(T)−k3​k⌉≤i≤⌊Star⁡(T)+k3​k⌋,\left\lceil\frac{{\rm Star}(T)-k}{3k}\right\rceil\leq i\leq\left\lfloor\frac{{\rm Star}(T)+k}{3k}\right\rfloor,

and

1t​‖a→−(q(i−1)​t+1​(T∖{⋆}),…,qi​t​(T∖{⋆}))‖22≤α.\frac{1}{t}\left\|\vec{a}-\left(q_{(i-1)t+1}(T\setminus\{\star\}),...,q_{it}(T\setminus\{\star\})\right)\right\|^{2}_{2}\leq\alpha.

We consider two types of algorithms:

  • •

    The one shot setting. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an algorithm that takes a multiset T⊆[n]∪{⋆}T\subseteq[n]\cup\{\star\} and returns a vector in ℝt\mathbb{R}^{t}. We say that this algorithm (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-solves the one shot variant of the BQQ,n,k,t{\rm BQ}_{Q,n,k,t} problem if for every TT, with probability at least 1−β1-\beta it holds that 𝒜⁡(T)\mathcal{A}(T) is α\alpha-accurate w.r.t. TT.

  • •

    The continual setting. Let r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} be a parameter. Consider an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that is initially instantiated with a multiset T⊆[n]∪{⋆}T\subseteq[n]\cup\{\star\} and returns a vector a→0∈ℝt\vec{a}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{t}. Then, in every round ℓ=1,2,…,r\ell=1,2,\dots,r, algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} obtains a “deletion request” zℓ∈[n]∪{⋆}z_{\ell}\in[n]\cup\{\star\} and returns an updated vector a→ℓ∈ℝt\vec{a}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{t}. We say that this algorithm (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-solves the BQQ,n,k,t{\rm BQ}_{Q,n,k,t} problem over rr rounds in the continual setting if for every TT and every adaptive strategy for selecting the zℓz_{\ell}’s, with probability at least 1−β1-\beta, for every ℓ\ell it holds that a→ℓ\vec{a}_{\ell} is α\alpha-accurate w.r.t. T∖{z1,…,zℓ}T\setminus\{z_{1},\dots,z_{\ell}\}.

Theorem B.2.

Let n,k,t∈ℕn,k,t\in\mathbb{N} and β,ε,δ∈[0,1]\beta,\varepsilon,\delta\in[0,1] be such that

k≥2ε​log⁡2βandt=o⁡(ε2​nlog⁡(1/δ))andn=ω⁡(log⁡(1/δ)​log⁡(1/β)ε2).k\geq\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{2}{\beta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad t=o\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}n}{\log(1/\delta)}\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad n=\omega\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)\log(1/\beta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

Then, for any set QQ of counting queries, there exists an (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP algorithm for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-solving the BQQ,n,k,t{\rm BQ}_{Q,n,k,t} problem in the one-shot setting for α=o⁡(n)\alpha=o(n).

Proof.

The construction is straightforward via the Laplace or Gaussian mechanism. Specifically, given the multiset TT, we first use the Laplace mechanism to find an appropriate index ii. That is, we compute:

i^←Star⁡(T)+Lap⁡(2ε)3​k.\hat{i}\leftarrow\frac{{\rm Star}(T)+{\rm Lap}(\frac{2}{\varepsilon})}{3k}.

This step satisfies (ε2,0)(\frac{\varepsilon}{2},0)-DP. Furthermore, the chosen index i^\hat{i} is valid (according to Definition B.1) whenever |Lap⁡(2ε)|≤k|{\rm Lap}(\frac{2}{\varepsilon})|\leq k, which happens with probability at least 1−β/21-\beta/2 provided that k≥2ε​log⁡2βk\geq\frac{2}{\varepsilon}\log\frac{2}{\beta}.

Given i^\hat{i}, all that remains is to answer to corresponding set of tt queries from QQ, which we again do via the Gaussian mechanism. Specifically, we answer each of these tt queries with independent noise sampled from 𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) for σ=16​t​log⁡(1/δ)ε\sigma=\frac{\sqrt{16t\log(1/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. By composition theorems for DP, this satisfies (ε2,δ)(\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\delta)-DP, and thus (again by composition), the overall algorithm satisfies (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)-DP as required.

Furthermore, by standard tail bounds for sums of independent squared normal random variables (aka the chi squared distribution), with probability at least 1−β/21-\beta/2, our average squared errors (denoted as α\alpha) satisfies

α≤σ2​(t+2​t​ln⁡(2/β)+2​ln⁡(2/β))t=16​log⁡(1/δ)​(t+2​t​ln⁡(2/β)+2​ln⁡(2/β))ε2,\alpha\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}\left(t+2\sqrt{t\ln(2/\beta)}+2\ln(2/\beta)\right)}{t}=\frac{16\log(1/\delta)\left(t+2\sqrt{t\ln(2/\beta)}+2\ln(2/\beta)\right)}{\varepsilon^{2}},

which is o⁡(n)o(n) provided that

t=o⁡(ε2​nlog⁡(1/δ))andn=ω⁡(log⁡(1/δ)​log⁡(1/β)ε2),t=o\left(\frac{\varepsilon^{2}n}{\log(1/\delta)}\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad n=\omega\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)\log(1/\beta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right),

as required. ∎

Theorem B.3.

Let n,k,t∈ℕn,k,t\in\mathbb{N} and α,β∈[0,1]\alpha,\beta\in[0,1] be such that α≤o⁡(n)\alpha\leq o(n). There exists a set of nn counting queries QQ and there exists an attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} such that the following holds. For any algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)-solving the BQQ,n,k,t{\rm BQ}_{Q,n,k,t} problem in the continual setting over r=⌈n/t⌉r=\lceil n/t\rceil rounds, and for any set D⊆[n]D\subseteq[n], if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is instantiated on the multiset TT containing DD as well as 3​k​r3kr copies of ⋆\star, and then interacts with ℬ\mathcal{B} over rr rounds (as in Definition B.1), then with probability at least 1−β1-\beta, at the end of the interaction the attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} outputs a set D^\hat{D} such that |D​△​D^|≤α\left|D\triangle\hat{D}\right|\leq\alpha.

Corollary B.4.

Combining Theorems B.2 and B.3, for n,k,t∈ℕn,k,t\in\mathbb{N} satisfying k≥ω⁡(1)k\geq\omega(1), and n=ω⁡(1)n=\omega\left(1\right), and t=o⁡(n)t=o\left(n\right), we get that

  1. 1.

    The BQQ,n,k,t{\rm BQ}_{Q,n,k,t} problem can be (o⁡(n),β)\left(o(n),\beta\right)-solved in the one shot setting while satisfying (o⁡(1),o⁡(1))\left(o(1),o(1)\right)-DP for any constant β\beta.

  2. 2.

    Any algorithm for (o⁡(n),β)\left(o(n),\beta\right)-solving the BQQ,n,k,t{\rm BQ}_{Q,n,k,t} problem in the continual setting allows an attacker controlling merely ω⁡(1)\omega(1) points to reconstruct almost all of the other points from the dataset with probability at least 1−β1-\beta.

Proof of Theorem B.3.

The construction follows from the results of Dwork and Yekhanin [2008], who presented a set of nn counting queries QQ and an attacker ℬDY\mathcal{B}_{\rm DY} such that for every set D⊆[n]D\subseteq[n], given approximate answers aq≈q⁡(D)a_{q}\approx q(D) for every qq in QQ satisfying

1n​∑q∈Q(aq−q⁡(D))2≤o⁡(n),\frac{1}{n}\sum_{q\in Q}(a_{q}-q(D))^{2}\leq o(n),

the attacker ℬDY\mathcal{B}_{\rm DY} can efficiently reconstruct a set D^\hat{D} with |D​△​D^|≤o⁡(n)\left|D\triangle\hat{D}\right|\leq o(n).

We implement this attacker in our setting as follows. Let TT be the multiset containing DD as well as 3​k​r3kr copies of ⋆\star. Now consider an attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} that plays against an algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} in the continual batch queries problem. Initially, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is instantiated with TT. Then, in every round, the attacker ℬ\mathcal{B} deletes 3​k3k copies of ⋆\star. By the definition of the BQ problem, this allows ℬ\mathcal{B} to obtain approximate answers aqa_{q} to every q∈Qq\in Q such that with probability at least 1−β1-\beta we have

1n​∑q∈Q(aq−q⁡(D))2≤o⁡(n).\frac{1}{n}\sum_{q\in Q}(a_{q}-q(D))^{2}\leq o(n).

This allows ℬ\mathcal{B} to run ℬDY\mathcal{B}_{\rm DY} to obtain a suitable reconstruction D^\hat{D}. ∎
